\nolinenumbers

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
## Every computed table and figure is the paper's own chunk, read from
## report.Rmd, and the paper's Markdown tables are copied from it by
## md_tab(), so neither can drift from the paper. Figure captions
## are restated in the chunk headers below, because read_chunk()
## carries code only; they match report.Rmd as of 2026-11-11.
rpt <- readLines('report.Rmd', warn = FALSE)
open <- grep('^```\\{r ', rpt)
close <- grep('^```\\s*$', rpt)
ends <- vapply(open, function(i) close[close > i][1], 0L)
labs <- sub('^```\\{r ([A-Za-z0-9_-]+).*$', '\\1', rpt[open])
keep <- labs != 'setup'
knitr::read_chunk(lines = rpt, labels = labs[keep],
                  from = open[keep] + 1L, to = ends[keep] - 1L)
## A Markdown table of the paper: its caption paragraph and rows.
md_tab <- function(lab) {
  i <- grep(sprintf('^Table: \\(\\\\#tab:%s\\)', lab), rpt)
  stopifnot(length(i) == 1)
  j <- i
  while (nzchar(rpt[j + 1])) j <- j + 1
  k <- j + 2
  stopifnot(startsWith(rpt[k], '|'))
  while (startsWith(rpt[k + 1], '|')) k <- k + 1
  cat(rpt[i:j], '', rpt[(j + 2):k], '', sep = '\n')
}
```

# Problem and approach {-}

Validating a predictive biomarker requires an interaction test. In an
aggregated N-of-1 design every participant is observed on and off
drug, and the power of that test must be estimated by simulation.
Paper 01 asks what the data-generating process (DGP) of such a
simulation should be. The DGP is a multivariate normal model in which
the predictive biomarker is a correlation with the drug response
(Hendrickson et al. 2020). The paper takes the open elements of the
DGP one at a time, compares the candidate choices, and judges them
against three requirements: a valid (positive-definite) joint
distribution, an interaction that survives carryover, and flexibility
to impose stress conditions. The
choices are collected as the recommended DGP, a step toward an optimal
one. The Hybrid design is the primary case. All simulations use the
default parameter values. The biomarker is assumed throughout to be
predictive only, not prognostic; the prognostic case is the subject of
a companion paper. A separate section lists the differences from the
DGP of Hendrickson et al. This summary reproduces every table and
figure of the paper. They follow the paper's order, except that the
table of matrices that are not positive definite, in the paper's
Appendix B.2, appears here in Stage 1. Each is generated by the same
code as in the paper.

# Methods

Table \@ref(tab:estimands) states which analysis targets which

```{r tab-estimands, results = 'asis'}
md_tab('estimands')
```

```{r tab-ademp, results = 'asis'}

```

# Results

## Stage 1. Feasibility of the joint distribution

Table \@ref(tab:nonpd) counts correlation matrices that are not
positive definite under the recommended DGP. At $c_{bm} = 0.6$, 75% of
them are infeasible. The recommended DGP stops on such a matrix rather
than repairing it. The choice rests on requirement 1, a valid joint
distribution.

```{r nonpd}
```

## Stage 2. The decaying biomarker-response correlation

Table \@ref(tab:closedform) gives closed-form power by half-life. Under
the constant rule E9 power falls to the test size at every positive
half-life. Under the decaying rule power stays near its no-carryover
value at 0.1 to 0.2 week and declines smoothly after. The choice of
the decaying rule rests on requirement 2, an interaction that survives
carryover.

```{r cfcount}
```

```{r closedform}
```

Figure \@ref(fig:powerfig) shows the same result as lines, with Monte
Carlo points on them.

```{r powerfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power (lines) against carryover half-life, with Monte Carlo estimates (points; 5,000 replicates per cell), under the constant rule (constant correlation after first exposure) and the decaying rule (correlation decaying at the carryover half-life). Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, compound symmetry; statistic E9.', out.width = '75%', fig.align = 'center'}
```

Figure \@ref(fig:gapfig) plots power against the on/off correlation
difference. Power depends on the correlation rule only through this
difference.

```{r gapfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power against the on/off correlation difference, with the positions of the two correlation rules. Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, E9.', out.width = '75%', fig.align = 'center'}
```

```{r fig4bg10data}
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bg10) shows the power of the recommended analysis
G10 (a random-intercept CAR(1) mixed model with an analysis half-life
chosen by AIC on the model without the interaction, and CR2 standard
errors) under the recommended DGP. At $N = 70$ without censoring,
Hybrid power is `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0)`,
`r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.1)` and `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.2)` at
half-lives of 0, 0.1 and 0.2 week. The open-label design has no
off-drug visit, so the interaction is not estimable under G10.

```{r fig4bg10, eval = have_f4, fig.cap = paste0('Power of the analysis G10 to detect the biomarker-by-treatment interaction under the recommended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$, decaying biomarker-response correlation, carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, default values). Rows within panels: censoring patterns, under which dropout rises with worsening; columns: carryover half-life; panels: trial design (N-of-1 is the Hybrid design) and total sample size. $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 250 replicates per cell (Monte Carlo SE at most ', g9f_mcse_max, '). Gray cells (n/e): the open-label design, in which every visit is on drug and the interaction is not estimable under G10.'), out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.2}
```

interaction is kept.

# Appendix A. Closed-form derivations {-}

## A.5 The separable structure {-}

Each step between visits contributes the following term to the
schedule term of the feasibility bound.

| Step | Term |
|---|---|
| on to on | $(1 - \rho_t)/(1 + \rho_t)$ |
| on to off | $\rho_t^2/(1 - \rho_t^2)$ |
| off to on | $1/(1 - \rho_t^2)$ |
| off to off | 0 |

# Conclusions

Three choices matter most. First, the biomarker-response correlation
must decay after discontinuation. If it stays constant after first
exposure, the interaction is absent among the post-baseline visits
under any carryover, and power falls nearly to the test size. With a
decaying biomarker-response correlation, power returns to its no-carryover value at
pharmacological half-lives and declines smoothly at half-lives of 0.5
week and above. Second, the serial correlation structure sets the
largest interaction the DGP can hold. A separable AR(1) structure at a
serial correlation of 0.7 raises the bound from 0.256 under compound
symmetry to 0.474. The value 0.7 is a convention, however. At 0.9 the
bound falls to `r rb_f(rb_min(0.9, 0))`, and the Hybrid design needs
`r pr_e9n(0.9, 'Hybrid', 0.25)` participants at $c_{bm} = 0.25$
instead of `r pr_e9n(0.7, 'Hybrid', 0.25)`. Third, a matrix outside
the bound should be refused rather than repaired.

We propose the recommended DGP as a reference for
simulation studies of these designs when the biomarker is predictive
only. Every parameter is labeled as a
default value, a choice or uncalibrated. Calibrating the serial
correlation, the drug-response SD and the symptom half-life is the
next step toward an optimal DGP.
